chapterTitle: Ch 36. Training for Robustness and Generality

concepts.title: Target Invariance in Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Target invariance assumes that the target outputs $y$ remain unchanged when the input $x$ undergoes specific transformations.
concepts.content: When applying data augmentation, we often assume that the target outputs $\mathbf{y}$ are invariant to the augmentations of the inputs $\mathbf{x}$. Let $y(\mathbf{x})$ be the true $\mathbf{y}$ for an input $\mathbf{x}$; then we assume that $y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$ for all $\theta$, meaning $y$ is invariant to the transformation $T$. For example, in scene classification, mirror augmentation is appropriate because mirroring a scene does not change its class label. However, in optical character recognition, mirror augmentation is unsuitable because the mirror image of a character like 'b' looks like 'd', meaning $y(\texttt{mirror}(\mathbf{x})) \neq y(\mathbf{x})$. Similarly, molecular data with chiral structures may behave differently from their mirror images, violating the invariance assumption.
concepts.motivation_md: Data augmentation relies on the assumption that certain transformations of the input data do not change the underlying label. Understanding target invariance helps practitioners choose augmentations that preserve the semantic meaning of the data, ensuring the model learns the correct relationships rather than being confused by transformations that alter the ground truth.
concepts.recap_md: - Target invariance occurs when $y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$, meaning the label is unaffected by the transformation.

concepts.title: Target Equivariance in Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Target equivariance involves transforming both inputs and targets simultaneously so that the relationship between them is preserved.
concepts.content: To handle cases where $y(\mathbf{x}) \neq y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$, we use a more advanced kind of data augmentation where we transform the $\mathbf{y}$ values at the same time as the $\mathbf{x}$ values using transforms $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$. This results in an augmented dataset of the form $\{T_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), T_{\mathcal{Y}}(\mathbf{y}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^M$. This requires that $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$ express an equivariance between the two domains, defined as $T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x),\theta_{\mathcal{Y}}) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x,\theta_{\mathcal{X}}))$ for all $\theta$. This is standard when $\mathbf{y}$ has spatial or temporal structure aligned with $\mathbf{x}$, such as semantic segmentation. In such cases, if we perform a random crop on the image $\mathbf{x}$, we must apply the same crop to the label map $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In many tasks, such as object detection or segmentation, the target label is spatially dependent on the input. If the input is cropped or rotated, the label must be updated accordingly. Equivariance ensures that the model learns the correct spatial mapping even when the input data is transformed.
concepts.recap_md: - Equivariance requires transforming the target $y$ in tandem with the input $x$ to maintain their relationship.

slots.motivation: In many tasks, such as object detection or segmentation, the target label is spatially dependent on the input. If the input is cropped or rotated, the label must be updated accordingly. Equivariance ensures that the model learns the correct spatial mapping even when the input data is transformed.

concepts.title: Domain Randomization
concepts.one_liner: Domain randomization broadens a model's experience by randomizing the parameters of a simulator rather than transforming a static dataset.
concepts.content: When data is generated by a simulator rather than sampled from a static dataset, we can apply domain randomization. Instead of adding random transformations to existing data points, we randomize the parameters of the simulator itself. For example, lighting conditions may be randomized so that each interaction with the simulation looks slightly different. The effect is analogous to data augmentation: it converts a narrow set of experiences (simulation with one lighting condition) into a much broader set of experiences (simulation with many different lighting conditions) for the model to learn from.
concepts.motivation_md: Simulators often fail to capture the full complexity of the real world, leading to a 'reality gap.' Domain randomization helps bridge this gap by exposing the model to a wide variety of simulated environments, making the resulting model more robust to variations it will encounter in real-world data.
concepts.recap_md: - Domain randomization involves varying simulator parameters like lighting or physics to create diverse training data.

concepts.title: Out-of-Distribution Data
concepts.one_liner: Out-of-distribution data refers to test cases that differ significantly in characteristics or distribution from the training data.
concepts.content:
Data augmentation works by broadening the distribution of training data to reduce the gap between training and test data. When test images look quite different from training data—for instance, having lower resolution or different object categories—we say the test data are out-of-distribution relative to the training data. Data augmentation adds variation to the training data, broadening its distribution so that the test data become more in-distribution. With sufficient augmentation, test data may eventually look like random samples from the training distribution.

![Data augmentation broadens the training distribution so that it might better cover the test cases. (a) Training data are from Caltech256 @griffin2007caltech and test data are from CIFAR100 @cifar100. The scatter plots show these data in a 2D feature space [the first two principle components (pcs) of CLIP @radford2021learning]. (b) Training data after `mirror` augmentations (random horizontal flips). (c) The same plus `crops` (crop then rescale to the original size). (d) The same plus `color jitter` (random shifts in color and contrast).](./figures/data_augmentation/data_aug_real_example.png){width="100%" #fig-data_augmentation-data_aug_real_example}
concepts.motivation_md: Models often fail when deployed because real-world data (test data) differs from the curated training set. Identifying and addressing out-of-distribution gaps through techniques like data augmentation is critical for building models that generalize to new environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Out-of-distribution (OOD) data is test data that does not match the statistical distribution of the training set.

concepts.title: Learned Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Learned data augmentation uses algorithms to discover complex transformations that a model should be invariant to, rather than coding them by hand.
concepts.content: While simple transformations like flipping or cropping are effective and easy to implement, they represent only a small fraction of possible transformations. For complex tasks like pedestrian detection, we might want a model to be invariant to variations in a pedestrian's pose. Because such variations are difficult to code by hand, we can use learning algorithms to learn how to augment our data and achieve the desired invariances. After learning, the model will be invariant (or equivariant) with respect to these discovered transformations.
concepts.motivation_md: Manual augmentation is limited by human intuition and coding effort. Learned augmentation allows the system to automatically find the most useful variations for a specific task, which is especially valuable for complex, high-dimensional transformations like human pose or lighting changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Learned data augmentation automates the discovery of transformations that improve model invariance.

slots.motivation: Manual augmentation is limited by human intuition and coding effort. concepts.title: Generative Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Generative data augmentation uses models like GANs or VAEs to create new training samples by perturbing latent variables.
concepts.content:
One way to perform learned data augmentation is to use generative models such as GANs or VAEs. These models are suitable because latent variables can control factors of variation. Given a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, an encoder $f_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, and a generator $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, we can create an augmented copy as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x} = g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{w}) \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathbf{w}$ is a small perturbation to the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$. If the generative model lacks an encoder, one can be trained via supervised learning on pairs $\{g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}), \mathbf{z}\}$. By using various settings of $\mathbf{w}$, such as Gaussian perturbations $\mathbf{w} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, we produce a set of output images that are slight variations of one another.

(see figure: Generative data augmentation `genaug`)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard augmentations are often restricted to simple geometric or color changes. Generative models can produce highly realistic and diverse variations of data that capture complex semantic changes, potentially providing a richer training signal than manual heuristics.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative data augmentation creates new samples by adding noise to the latent representation of existing data.

slots.motivation: Standard augmentations are often restricted to simple geometric or color changes. Generative models can produce highly realistic and diverse variations of data that capture complex semantic changes, potentially providing a richer training signal than manual heuristics.
slots.key_passage: - Generative data augmentation creates new samples by adding noise to the latent representation of existing data.

concepts.title: Circularity in Learned Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Circularity in learned augmentation occurs when the augmentation model is trained on the same data it is intended to augment.
concepts.content: Training a generative model $g_{\theta}$ on a dataset $X$ and then using $g_{\theta}$ to augment $X$ for training a function $f$ introduces a circularity. If we denote the learner as a function $L$ that maps data to a learned function $f$, then without augmentation $f = L(X)$. With augmentation, $f = L(\tilde{X})$. If $\tilde{X}$ is generated by an algorithm like $\texttt{genaug}(X)$, then $\tilde{X}$ is simply a function of $X$. This implies the existence of a new learner $\tilde{L} = L \circ \texttt{genaug}$ such that $f = \tilde{L}(X)$. Thus, a learning algorithm using unaugmented data can be functionally equivalent to one using augmented data when the augmentation itself is derived from that same data.
concepts.motivation_md: It is important to recognize that learned augmentation doesn't 'create' new information out of thin air if it's trained on the same set. Understanding this circularity helps researchers distinguish between true information gain and complex forms of regularization.
concepts.recap_md: - Circularity occurs when augmented data $\tilde{X}$ is a deterministic function of the original data $X$.

slots.motivation: It is important to recognize that learned augmentation doesn't 'create' new information out of thin air if it's trained on the same set. Understanding this circularity helps researchers distinguish between true information gain and complex forms of regularization.
slots.key_passage: - Circularity occurs when augmented data $\tilde{X}$ is a deterministic function of the original data $X$.

concepts.title: Robust Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Robust optimization is a general approach in optimization where models are trained to perform well under adversarial or worst-case conditions.
concepts.content: Robust optimization is a general approach in the optimization literature that encompasses techniques like adversarial training. It is used for various purposes, including training generative adversarial networks, encouraging exploration in reinforcement learning, and training agents to compete against others. The core idea is to optimize for performance that is resilient to variations or adversarial perturbations in the input or environment.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard optimization might produce models that are fragile to small changes. Robust optimization seeks to ensure that a model's performance remains stable even when faced with the worst-case scenarios or noisy environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Robust optimization focuses on maintaining performance under perturbations or adversarial conditions.

concepts.title: Data Augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Data augmentation expands a dataset by adding synthetic versions of data points created through random transformations.
concepts.content:
Data augmentation expands a dataset by adding random transformations of each datapoint. For each $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}$ pair in the original dataset, you add $M$ new synthetic pairs $\{T(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{j=1}^M$, where $T$ is a transformation function with stochastic parameters $\theta$. For example, $T$ might be a `crop` function with $\theta$ representing coordinates.

(see figure: A few common types of data augmentation.)

By mapping a smaller dataset to a larger one, data augmentation simulates the effect of adding more real data. It is a critical tool in machine learning because larger datasets generally lead to better performance.

[FIGURE:d88031ceb8315562 | A flowchart showing the process of data augmentation. It starts with a 'Small dataset' represented by the set {x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N, which passes through a 'Data augmentation' block...]
concepts.motivation_md: Data is the fuel for machine learning, but collecting real-world data is expensive. Data augmentation allows us to bake domain knowledge (like 'a cat is still a cat if cropped') into the model while artificially increasing the dataset size.
concepts.recap_md:
- It creates synthetic training examples using stochastic transformations like cropping or rotating.
 - It effectively increases dataset size, which typically improves model performance.
 - The labels remain the same for the transformed versions of the original data points.

concepts.title: Multitask Training
concepts.one_liner: Multitask training defines a new task for which multiple specific tasks are special cases, allowing the model to be trained on data from all tasks.
concepts.content: Because we have finite data for any given task, it can help to share data between tasks. One approach is to not just broaden the data but to also broaden the task by defining a new task, $AB$, for which tasks $A$ and $B$ are special cases. Then we can train $AB$ on both the data for task $A$ and for task $B$. An example of a metatask like $AB$ is data imputation. For instance, predicting missing color channels is the colorization problem (task $A$), while predicting a chunk of pixels masked out of an image is the inpainting problem (task $B$). We can train a joint colorization–inpainting model by setting up both as data imputation and training a general data imputation model on both sets of training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Data scarcity is a common bottleneck in deep learning. Multitask training solves this by allowing a model to borrow data from related tasks, improving generalization and efficiency.
concepts.recap_md:
- Define a broad metatask that encompasses multiple specific sub-tasks. 
- Train a single model on the combined datasets of all included tasks. 
- Use shared representations to improve performance on tasks with limited data.

concepts.title: Data Imputation Framework
concepts.one_liner: Data imputation is an incredibly general framework where models learn to predict missing data, such as color channels or masked pixels.
concepts.content: Data imputation is an incredibly general framework. For example, predicting missing color channels is the colorization problem, and predicting a chunk of pixels masked out of an image is the inpainting problem. We can train a joint colorization–inpainting model if we simply set up both as data imputation and train a general data imputation model. This model can be trained on both colorization training data and inpainting training data. This raises the question of which vision problems can be formulated as data imputation, and which ones cannot.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a unified way to frame diverse self-supervised tasks, allowing models to learn from the structure of the data itself without explicit labels for every sub-task.
concepts.recap_md:
- Formulates learning as predicting missing or corrupted parts of the input data. 
- Acts as a metatask for specific problems like colorization and inpainting. 
- Enables joint training across different types of data missingness.

prereq.rationale: Target invariance is the foundational assumption for most basic data augmentation techniques.
Target equivariance is a more advanced kind of data augmentation used when labels must change along with inputs.
Learned data augmentation is an automated approach to discovering effective augmentation strategies.
Learned augmentation techniques are often designed to discover and enforce specific target invariances that are hard to hand-code.
The circularity problem arises specifically when a generative model is used to augment the same data it was trained on.

overlay.rationale: Both techniques aim to improve model performance when data for a specific task is limited.
Data imputation is a concrete example of a "metatask" that combines multiple specific vision problems.
Target equivariance is used when the assumption of target invariance (where the label remains unchanged) does not hold.
Domain randomization is described as the simulation-based version of data augmentation, achieving similar goals through different means.
Data augmentation is specifically used to broaden the training distribution so that previously out-of-distribution test data becomes in-distribution.
Generative augmentation is a specific implementation of the broader concept of learned data augmentation.
